# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
This comment does useful forensic work, but its conclusion goes beyond its evidence.

Sections 1–5 are valuable. The attrition finding in particular is new: the Halden paper says the nine withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase", but the microdata show seven of them happened after the reduced schedule began. If that's right, Halden should issue a correction. The arithmetic in Table 2 and the revenue deflation checks out:
- 95.1 / 0.8 → +18.9%
- 98.4 / 0.859 → +14.6%
- 95.4 / 0.861 → +10.8%
- 1.014 / 1.041 → −2.6%

The problems are in §6–8 and in how the abstract and conclusion summarise the results.

## 1. "Entirely an artifact" isn't supported, even by the comment's own numbers

- **The comment's own estimate is still positive.** After its corrections, the gain in output per actual hour is +10.8%. To call this "entirely an artifact", the comment rests everything on the novelty argument (§6), which is the weakest section. The abstract says the residual is "plausibly" novelty. The conclusion turns that into "entirely".
- **The claim covers far more than one pilot.** "The per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes" generalises from one uncontrolled pilot to the whole literature.
- **The comment cites Varden selectively.** It calls Varden's counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature". But the same trial's case-processing stratum found +12.5% per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4). That estimate used the methods the comment itself recommends: randomisation, record-based output and timesheet hours. Only the eighteen-month follow-up is missing. The comment can't treat one stratum of a trial as the most reliable evidence and ignore the other stratum, which contradicts its conclusion.
- **"Burden of proof" doesn't justify "entirely".** Saying a gain hasn't been shown to last is reasonable. Concluding that it is entirely an artifact is a different claim.

A defensible conclusion would be something like:
> "The reported gain falls by more than half under correction; whether the remainder is durable is unknown."

## 2. The abstract says attrition was corrected, but it wasn't

The abstract says "correcting the first three" problems, including attrition, gives 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only the output measure and the hours. The 17 organisations behind the 10.8% are all survivors.

Attrition also can't plausibly remove the residual on its own. Suppose withdrawers were added back in proportion: 9 of 70 is about 13%, or roughly 2.5 organisations added to the subset of 17. Assume their hours fell like everyone else's. For per-hour output to fall to zero gain, pooled output would have to drop to 86.1. That requires the withdrawers' output index to be about 23, a 77% collapse.

Withdrawers probably did badly, but nothing suggests anything close to that. The microdata may include withdrawers' monthly indexes for their first one or two months. If so, the comment should use them to put bounds on the effect rather than only asserting the direction of the bias.

## 3. The novelty argument is weak, and the data to test it are available

- **The comment relies on one self-report measure.** It rightly distrusts manager self-reports of output, then rests its central claim on employee self-reports of energy. Energy is also not output.
- **Two points don't make a trend.** The extrapolation uses two survey waves. Taken literally, it predicts that energy returns to baseline around month 8.7, not "around month ten". Linear decay from two waves is not a reliable basis either way. At month six, energy was still 0.29 SD above baseline.
- **Novelty can be tested directly.** The pilot collected a monthly output index. If the gain were novelty, output per hour should decline over months 1–6, at least in the 17 organisations with records and time tracking. The comment has the data to check this and doesn't.
- **Varden ran longer.** Its case-processing gain was measured at nine months. Varden staff also didn't choose the change, which weakens the "staff chose and welcomed it" part of the novelty story. Varden doesn't rule out novelty, but the comment should engage with it.

## 4. §7 misdescribes the Varden meetings analysis and holds it to a double standard

- **What Varden actually said.** The Varden authors said explicitly that the analysis was unregistered and based on seven offices, and that "a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism". They also registered a confirmatory test. They did not present it as an established mechanism. The comment implies they did.
- **"Selected after the results were known" is inaccurate.** The data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results existed. The seven offices are also a pre-specified randomisation stratum, not a subgroup chosen after the fact.
- **The comment applies a double standard.** Its own novelty explanation rests on two survey waves and is used to draw a strong conclusion. The meetings explanation rests on thin but different evidence and is dismissed. Meetings are also directly relevant to the residual: if the gain came from cutting low-value time, it would be durable, not novelty. Halden's own interviews point the same way, with 47 of 58 managers mentioning meeting cuts.

The valid criticisms of the meetings analysis are these:
- There is no pre-period meetings data, so the treated-vs-control difference could predate the trial.
- With seven offices, r = 0.71 has a 95% CI of roughly −0.09 to 0.95.

Making those points would be stronger than the current framing.

## 5. The hours breakdown in §3 doesn't add up

The comment reports four days of +0.7 hours plus 1.6 hours on the day off. Either way of reading that gives about 36.4–36.6 hours a week:
- Relative to scheduled 8-hour days: 4 × 8.7 + 1.6 = 36.4.
- Relative to baseline days of about 8.06 hours: 4 × 8.76 + 1.6 = 36.6.

The reported pilot average is 34.6 hours. For that figure to hold with 1.6 hours on the day off, the extra time per day can only be about +0.2–0.25 hours. One of the numbers is wrong, or the two components come from different subsets of organisations. This needs fixing, because the hours correction carries most of the drop in the estimate.

## 6. Record-based output has its own limits

- **Billable hours is partly an input.** "Billable hours delivered" is one of the record types. It is largely tied to hours worked, so using it as output builds in little or no per-hour gain by construction. Report results with and without the organisations that use it.
- **Records may be narrower than managers' judgements.** Records like tickets closed or units produced may miss quality or scope that a manager's index captures. The direction of the gap (managers higher in 19 of 23) is persuasive. Treating the records as ground truth needs a sentence of justification.
- **Table 1 needs a confidence interval** for the −3.8-point difference. A sign test on 19 of 23 would also do.
- **Selection into the record subset.** Records were submitted voluntarily. The Data note acknowledges this, but the abstract and conclusion state the subset results as if they described the whole pilot.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Retail sample size.** The retail and hospitality figure from records (−11.2%) comes from three organisations. Say so in §5.
- **Wrong deflator.** CPI is the wrong deflator for business revenue; sector output prices would be better. The direction of the point probably holds, so a footnote is enough.
- **Mixed metrics in the conclusion.** "Where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output" refers to output per employee. The rest of the paper is about output per hour. Make the switch explicit, especially since Varden's counter stratum showed a per-hour *rise* alongside the fall per employee.

## Overall

The comment should keep §1–5 and the recommendations, which are sound. It should:
- correct the abstract's claim that attrition was adjusted for,
- fix the hours breakdown,
- test novelty with the monthly output data instead of inferring it from energy scores,
- describe the Varden meetings analysis accurately,
- deal with Varden's case-processing result,
- replace "entirely an artifact" with a claim the evidence supports: the Halden gain is overstated by more than half, and the durability of the remainder is unknown.

I can draft a referee report or a reply-to-comment based on these notes.
